narration:
The notice comes away with a dry rip, leaving the corner still pinned to the board. In the lantern light of the wayside square it's quiet. A few carters are dozing against their wagon wheels, a woman is banking a brazier, and a boy is minding two mules. When your voice carries across the cobbles, every one of them looks up.

The organiser is a lean man in an ink-stained coat with a ledger tucked under his arm. He doesn't flinch. He watches you finish, then turns his head slightly, the way a man does when he wants the crowd to hear his answer.

"Cheat," he says, as if he's trying the word out. "Thief. All right. I'm Edric Vell and I've posted work at this crossroads for nine years. You're the first person I've seen tonight." He nods at the paper crumpled in your fist. "Name one honest person I've robbed and I'll pay them here, in front of everyone. If you can't, that notice is a guide's job. Bring it back or take the work. Tearing it down doesn't put money in anybody's pocket."

Some of the carters chuckle. Not all of them do.

By the brazier, a broad woman with soot on her forearms keeps her eyes on Vell. "Took three weeks to get my fen-haul money last spring," she mutters, loud enough to be heard. Then she goes back to her coals.

Vell's jaw tightens for a moment, and then he's composed again.

"Come back whenever you like," he tells you. "I'm always here."

Smoothed against your palm, the notice reads: *GUIDE WANTED: two wagons, Sallow Fen road to Marrow Ford. Three days. 12 silver on safe arrival. Apply to E. Vell.*

narration:
The lantern light of the square is behind you within a few hundred paces. Nobody calls after you. The road runs east between hedges black against the stars. You walk until the hedges give out and the air turns wet and sour with standing water, then sleep a few hours in the lee of a gatepost with your coat pulled tight.

Day one is open farmland that gets lower with every mile. Ditches become dikes, and the dikes become reed beds taller than you. The road is now a raised causeway of packed clay and old timber, with deep wagon ruts filled with brown water. You have no food and no water skin. By afternoon your stomach has stopped complaining and gone quiet, which is worse. You drink from a clear runnel off a culvert and hope for the best.

On the morning of day two the causeway goes under. For half a mile the road is a sheet of still water dotted with reed tussocks. Somewhere beneath it there is solid ground, and on either side there isn't.

narration:
The organiser is closing up for the night. She's a broad, weathered woman with a slate under one arm and chalk dust on her sleeves, and she's lifting the lantern off its hook when you ask. She hangs it back up.

"Best pay?" She taps the board without looking, like she knows every pin by heart. "Fence mending at the Dunmore farm pays three silver a day. Quarry hauling pays four, if your back's good." Her finger moves to a crisp sheet near the top, newer than the rest. "This one pays twenty-five silver for one job."

The notice is in a merchant's tidy hand: *GUIDE WANTED. Lower Fen crossing to Tallow Mill. One wool cart, two persons. Departing at first light. Ask for I. Callow at the Lantern.*

"Idris Callow. He's a wool factor and he's been sleeping at the inn across the square for three nights." She nods toward a low building with one window still lit. "The spring flood took the bridge road. The long way round is four days, and his buyer at the mill won't wait four days."

She looks you over, and her eyes stop for a moment on the compass at your belt.

"It pays best because nobody local wants it. The flood moved the channels and tore up half the marker poles. Old Benning used to guide that crossing. He looked at it after the water went down and said he's too old to learn a new fen." She shrugs. "If you can read ground and keep a heading in the mist, it's honest money. Callow pays me my cut, not you. If you go to him, tell him Hesper sent you, so I know who to chalk off."

The light is still on at the Lantern.

narration:
Hesper shakes her head before you've finished the sentence, though not unkindly.

"I don't hire. I post." She slides the slate out from under her arm, wets her thumb, and chalks a line under a column of names: *ROWAN — FEN — CALLOW.* "That's you written down. It means I sent you, not that he's taken you. He'll want to look at you first. Three nights he's waited, so he'll look hard."

She tears a strip off the bottom of an old notice, a fence-mending job someone already filled, scrawls *H.V. sends this one* on the back, and holds it out.

"As for what counts as done, that's his to say and yours to agree to. The notice says one cart and two people to Tallow Mill. That's all I know." She taps the slate against her palm. "But I've watched enough jobs go sour on this board to tell you what to settle before you shake on it. Does done mean the mill gate, or the buyer's yard? What happens if the ox goes lame and you turn back halfway? Who pays if the cart goes in? Merchants like to pay at the far end. Get half now if he'll give it. Get the rest in writing if he won't."

She lifts the lantern off its hook again.

"He's tidy, Callow. He'll write it down if you ask him to. So ask."

Across the square, the Lantern's window is still lit.

narration:
The Lantern's door is unbarred. Inside, one man sits at a table by the lit window with a ledger, an ink pot and a cold supper he hasn't touched. He's lean and neat, his cuffs turned back so they stay clean. He reads Hesper's chit twice, then looks at you longer than he looked at the chit. His eyes go to the compass and your boots, and he seems to like the boots better.

"Idris Callow. Three nights I've sat here." He turns to a clean page. "As posted, then. I'll write it down, because I don't shake on things I can't read back."

His pen is quick and small:

*Rowan to guide one wool cart, ox, carter and I. Callow across the Lower Fen to Tallow Mill. Done when the cart stands in Garrow's yard at the mill with the wool dry and both persons whole. 25 silver: 5 now, 20 on arrival. If the crossing is judged impassable and we turn back together, the 5 stands and nothing more is owed. Wagon on the cart road at first light.*

He signs it, turns it round to face you, and puts five silver on the page.

"My carter is Dell. He's young and doesn't talk much, but he's good with the ox. Sleep if you can."

---

The square is grey and dripping before dawn. Dell is a big lad with a sheepskin over his shoulders. He nods once and clicks the ox on. The cart road drops into the fen within the hour. The mist lies chest-high, so you all walk with your heads above it while the ox walks inside it.

For the first mile the old marker poles stand where they should, tarred and white-banded. Then they stop. One leans almost flat with its band pointing at open water. Past it there's a stretch of reed and brown pools, and the track you were following just ends.

Callow checks the date in his book. Dell waits for you to point the way.

You take a bearing, kneel to look at the reed stems and the colour of the water, and pick a line.

narration:
Hesper and her board are six miles behind you, across the mist. The job isn't finished, and nothing you can hand over would show that it is. You're still in the Lower Fen, and the fen has just made that very clear.

The line you picked holds for most of a mile. The reed stands up straight and the ground gives a little underfoot, but it springs back. Then the ox puts a foot down and pulls it up black to the knee. A moment later the near wheel drops with a long, sucking sound. It sinks to the hub in fresh silt the flood laid down, grey and smooth as porridge. The cart tilts. The bales slide against their ropes and stop. They're still dry, but they're leaning hard.

Dell is at the ox's head right away, one hand flat on its neck. "Don't pull," he says. "Axle'll go."

Callow doesn't say anything. He opens his book and looks at the date, then at the wheel, then at you.

You can see what's around you now that you're standing still. Behind you there's firmer reed, maybe twenty paces back, where the stems grow thick and pale. Off to the left, west, there's a channel that isn't on any map anyone has given you. It's new, with brown water moving slowly and sheer cut banks. There's no brush within reach worth the name, but the cart bed has planks and the bales have rope.

Bettany's ledger is still in your pack. You can collect the three coins at the board when you get back. Callow pays the twenty silver in Garrow's yard, not before.

The ox shifts and blows. The mist is starting to thin.

narration:
Hesper isn't here. She's six miles back across the fen, probably still asleep above her board. She has never paid you anything, either. She takes her cut from employers, not from the people they hire. So there is no first payment to collect twice. The only money you've had for this job is Callow's five silver earnest, and it's in your purse.

The only people here are a stuck cart, an ox standing in silt up to its hocks, and two men watching you.

Callow has heard you talking to nobody. He closes his book on one finger to keep the page.

"If you're counting money," he says, quietly and evenly, "count it in Garrow's yard. That's where it's written." He nods at the sunk wheel. "Right now I'd rather know what we're doing about that."

Dell hasn't moved from the ox's head. The animal shifts its weight and the mud sucks at its feet. Dell keeps talking to it under his breath and keeps one eye on you.

The mist is thinning fast. You can see farther now. The pale, thick reed twenty paces back looks like firm ground. Westward, the brown channel's cut banks drop a man's height to slow water. The cart bed has planks, and the bales are tied down with rope. Through a gap in the mist the sun is a dull coin above the reeds, already higher than Callow would like.

The wheel is still sunk to the hub, and the wool is still dry.
